PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 78 — Lesson 102: Stroke & TIA Management

FNP-level goal: Recognize possible acute stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), arrange emergency evaluation without delay, support cause-directed secondary prevention after the acute phase, and coordinate safe recovery, function, and caregiver follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify common and atypical stroke/TIA symptoms and distinguish time-sensitive emergency recognition from outpatient secondary prevention.
  • Explain why a TIA is a warning event requiring urgent evaluation even when symptoms resolve.
  • Organize a cause-directed secondary-prevention framework that includes vascular risk factors, antithrombotic safety, rhythm/carotid evaluation, and medication access.
  • Assess poststroke deficits, dysphagia/aspiration risk, mood/cognition, falls, pain, caregiver burden, and rehabilitation needs.
  • Recognize red flags for recurrent stroke, hemorrhage, worsening neurologic deficit, or unsafe discharge follow-up.

Part 1 — Acute Neurologic Symptoms Are an Emergency Problem

Stroke symptoms can include sudden facial droop, unilateral arm or leg weakness/numbness, speech or language difficulty, vision loss or diplopia, severe imbalance, new confusion, or a sudden severe headache. FAST is a useful public recognition tool: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. It does not capture every posterior-circulation or atypical presentation, so sudden focal neurologic change, new severe imbalance, or acute visual symptoms still require emergency consideration.

Time last known well, medication/anticoagulant exposure, baseline function, symptom onset/trajectory, glucose when available, and vital signs are important information—but should not delay emergency transport or emergency evaluation. Do not advise a patient with possible acute stroke to drive themselves.

Part 2 — TIA Is Not “Nothing Happened”

A TIA is a transient neurologic deficit caused by focal ischemia without infarction on imaging. Symptoms may fully resolve, but the event signals elevated near-term stroke risk. A resolved episode of unilateral weakness, aphasia, monocular vision loss, or another focal deficit still needs urgent emergency or stroke-capable evaluation. Avoid falsely reassuring labels such as “just dizziness” or “mini-stroke” without a focused neurologic and vascular assessment.

Part 3 — Define the Mechanism Before Choosing the Long-Term Plan

Secondary prevention is not a single prescription. Ischemic stroke/TIA may be cardioembolic (for example, AF), large-artery atherosclerotic, small-vessel, dissection-related, or of another/uncertain mechanism. Etiologic evaluation may involve brain/vascular imaging, ECG and rhythm monitoring, echocardiographic evaluation when indicated, and targeted laboratory studies. The FNP supports timely completion of this workup, obtains/acts on results, and coordinates neurology, cardiology, vascular, and rehabilitation care as appropriate.

AF is an important and treatable stroke mechanism. When no other cause is found, longer-term rhythm monitoring may increase detection of occult AF. Carotid disease can also be an important and potentially treatable cause in selected patients. The key principle is cause-directed prevention, not empiric use of every antithrombotic medication.

Part 4 — Antithrombotic and Vascular-Risk Safety

Many patients need an antiplatelet or anticoagulant strategy unless contraindicated, but the correct regimen depends on stroke subtype, AF or another cardioembolic source, coronary/stent history, timing, bleeding risk, kidney function, procedures, and current guidance. With limited exceptions, combining antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is not a routine long-term secondary-prevention strategy. Dual antiplatelet therapy is not a universal or indefinite plan. Verify the hospital/neurology plan rather than guessing, and reconcile all OTC NSAIDs, supplements, and duplicate agents.

Blood pressure, lipid, diabetes, tobacco, diet, physical activity, sleep, alcohol/substance exposure, and medication adherence are modifiable secondary-prevention domains. When a stroke occurs despite a prescribed medication, first determine whether it was taken consistently and what barrier caused nonadherence before assuming the drug “failed.” Cost, cognitive impairment, dysphagia, depression, caregiver support, and health literacy may be the real clinical problem.

Part 5 — Recovery Care Is Clinical Care

At postdischarge follow-up, assess new or worsening weakness, speech/language, vision, gait, sensation, swallowing, nutrition/hydration, continence, pain/spasticity, fatigue, sleep, falls, skin integrity, mood, anxiety, cognition, and caregiver strain. Dysphagia can cause aspiration, malnutrition, and medication-administration problems. Functional status determines whether the treatment plan is safe at home. Medication lists, driving/work guidance, rehabilitation attendance, home equipment, and follow-up appointments all need confirmation.

Depression, anxiety, pseudobulbar affect, apathy, and cognitive changes are common after stroke and can impair recovery and adherence. Ask directly, use appropriate screening, assess safety, and connect patients and caregivers with behavioral-health, social-work, therapy, community, and rehabilitation resources.

Part 6 — Emergency and Urgent Escalation

Emergency evaluation is required for any new or recurrent focal neurologic deficit, sudden severe headache, decreased consciousness, seizure with persistent deficit, head trauma while anticoagulated, acute severe hypertension with neurologic symptoms, or rapid functional decline. New headache, vomiting, confusion, or neurologic worsening after a recent stroke may indicate complications and should not be managed by routine portal message. After discharge, uncertainty about a patient’s ability to swallow, obtain medications, ambulate safely, or recognize emergency symptoms also warrants urgent team intervention.

Clinical Case

A 68-year-old reports a 15-minute episode yesterday of right-arm weakness and word-finding difficulty that completely resolved. The patient has hypertension and smoking exposure and asks for a routine visit next week.

FNP reasoning: transient focal deficits are concerning for TIA. Resolution does not make this safe for delayed routine follow-up. Arrange urgent emergency/stroke-capable evaluation, document last known well and medication history, and ensure the patient does not drive. Long-term prevention will depend on the identified mechanism and complete risk-factor plan.

FNP Stroke/TIA Framework

  1. Recognize and triage: sudden focal neurologic symptoms = emergency evaluation; note time last known well without delaying transport.
  2. Do not minimize TIA: transient deficits need urgent evaluation because near-term stroke risk remains elevated.
  3. Clarify cause: coordinate rhythm, vascular, cardiac, imaging, and neurology evaluation as indicated.
  4. Prevent recurrence: mechanism-specific antithrombotic plan plus BP, lipid, diabetes, tobacco, lifestyle, and access management.
  5. Support recovery: assess function, swallowing, falls, mood/cognition, caregivers, rehabilitation, and home safety.

High-Yield Summary

Possible stroke: new focal neurologic symptoms are an emergency—even if symptoms are atypical.
TIA: symptoms resolving does not remove urgency.
Secondary prevention: is based on stroke mechanism; do not apply antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapies indiscriminately.
At follow-up: assess both recurrence risk and function, swallowing, cognition, mood, falls, caregivers, and medication access.
FNP standard: act fast for new symptoms and close every poststroke safety loop.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Acute stroke/TIA triage, diagnostic workup, antithrombotic selection, risk-factor targets, rehabilitation, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
